name: Georgia pro-EU protests and crackdown
parties: Georgian Dream government of Bidzina Ivanishvili
trigger: The Georgian Dream government announced on 28 November 2024 that it was suspending EU accession talks until 2028, weeks after a disputed parliamentary election.
summary: Daily protests outside parliament in Tbilisi began in late November 2024 after Georgian Dream froze EU accession talks following a disputed election. The government responded with riot police, new laws restricting assembly, media and NGOs, and prosecutions of opposition leaders, journalists and protesters. By October 2026 the ruling party was seeking a Constitutional Court ban on the main opposition parties while nightly rallies continued.

history.status: As of mid-October 2026 protesters have gathered outside parliament for roughly 690 consecutive days, and the 44th weekly Saturday march on 17 October demanded the release of around 150 people civil society counts as prisoners of conscience, including journalist Mzia Amaglobeli. The Constitutional Court accepted Georgian Dream's lawsuit to ban five opposition parties on 13 October and opens hearings in Batumi on 21-23 October; a judge resigned after being refused recusal. On 19 October a journalist was jailed for 30 days for criticising government figures online.

history.status: After Georgian Dream suspended EU accession talks on 28 November 2024, nightly protests in Tbilisi were met with water cannon, tear gas and hundreds of detentions, and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze warned of further arrests. name: Madagascar Gen Z uprising and military takeover
parties: CAPSAT army unit / Col. Michael Randrianirina
trigger: Youth protests over chronic water and electricity cuts began in Antananarivo on 25 September 2025 and escalated into demands for Rajoelina's resignation.
summary: Gen Z-led demonstrations over power and water outages in late September 2025 grew into a nationwide uprising; the elite CAPSAT unit sided with protesters, Rajoelina fled abroad, and Colonel Michael Randrianirina was sworn in as transitional president on 17 October 2025. The African Union suspended Madagascar and the UN condemned the takeover. A military-led transition now runs to elections promised by 2027, while activists accuse the new authorities of reverting to repression.

history.status: As of mid-October 2026 the junta remains in control one year after taking power; the army says a draft constitution will be ready by May 2027 ahead of a referendum, with a presidential election pencilled in for September 2027. Six Gen Z activists were jailed after an April 2026 march demanding an election date, on charges Amnesty called vague. Anniversary coverage (24 September and 12-19 October 2026) reports activists saying the promised 'refoundation' has not materialised, and notes growing Russian influence over the transitional government.

name: Serbia anti-corruption protests
parties: Student-led protest movement and Student List
Serbian government and SNS of Aleksandar Vucic
trigger: The collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad on 1 November 2024 killed 16 people and set off student-led protests against corruption and state capture.
summary: Student-led demonstrations against corruption and the rule of President Aleksandar Vucic have continued almost without interruption since November 2024, becoming the largest protest movement in Serbia's post-Milosevic history. Prime Minister Milos Vucevic resigned in January 2025, and the movement's central demand became a snap election. Vucic resigned as president on 27 September 2026 to run for prime minister in a snap parliamentary election on 25 October 2026, which the students are contesting with their own list.

history.status: As of 19 October 2026 Serbia is in the final week before the 25 October snap parliamentary election, called after Vucic resigned as president on 27 September (pardoning dozens of protest-related suspects minutes beforehand) to run for prime minister; Ana Brnabic is acting president. Election-related protest walks began on 16 October and converge on a rally in Belgrade's Slavija Square on 22 October, with polls suggesting the Student List could win. Digital-rights groups reported on 19 October that the University of Belgrade rector and an organised-crime prosecutor were targeted by spyware.

name: Iran nationwide uprising and crackdown
parties: Islamic Republic security forces and judiciary
trigger: Protests over currency collapse and economic hardship began in late December 2025 and spread nationwide into the largest anti-government uprising since 1979.
summary: Economic protests that began in December 2025 escalated in January 2026 into a nationwide uprising, met by live fire, an internet blackout and mass arrests; activist groups documented more than 7,000 deaths and over 26,000 detentions, while state TV acknowledged 3,117 dead. Through 2026 the judiciary has conducted mass trials and executions of detained protesters. Sporadic protests, notably by retirees and workers, continue despite the repression.

history.status: Amnesty International reported that five men convicted over the January 2026 protests were executed between 30 September and 5 October 2026 after torture-tainted trials, with at least 20 more protest-related prisoners facing imminent execution after the Supreme Court upheld their sentences; Iran International counts more than 70 political prisoners executed since December 2025. On 18 October 2026 retirees protested in Tehran, Rasht, Kermanshah, Isfahan, Shush and Ahvaz over pensions, with crowds in Rasht also chanting against the executions. Street mobilisation remains far below January levels under heavy security.

In mid-September unemployed graduates in Sidi Bouzid, Kasserine and Gabes demanded public-sector hiring. On 17 October 2026 the UGTT union, opposition parties and civil society staged the biggest anti-Saied march in years in Tunis.

Demonstrators demanded the release of jailed critics, an end to attacks on union rights and solutions to the economic crisis, shortages and power and water cuts. name: US anti-ICE and 'No Kings' protests
parties: No Kings coalition, immigrant-rights and 'ICE Out' protesters
Trump administration, ICE and federal agents
trigger: Mass immigration raids and the federalisation of the National Guard in Los Angeles in June 2025 triggered nationwide anti-ICE protests and the first 'No Kings' day of action on 14 June 2025.
summary: Since June 2025 the United States has seen recurring nationwide mobilisations against President Trump's immigration crackdown and use of executive power, including 'No Kings' days in June and October 2025 and March 2026 with millions of participants. National Guard deployments to Los Angeles, Washington DC, Memphis, Chicago and Portland drew litigation; the Supreme Court blocked the Chicago deployment on 23 December 2025 and Trump withdrew Guard troops from Chicago, Los Angeles and Portland in January 2026. The most violent phase came during 'Operation Metro Surge' in Minneapolis, where federal agents shot dead two US citizens, Renee Good (7 January 2026) and Alex Pretti (24 January 2026), prompting weeks of protests until the operation ended on 12 February 2026.

history.status: On 17 October 2026 the No Kings coalition staged more than 3,000 largely peaceful rallies nationwide framed as an early-voting 'day of action' ahead of the November midterms, with turnout smaller than earlier rounds in some cities and speakers again condemning ICE tactics. No National Guard deployments were tied to the rallies; the Minneapolis surge ended on 12 February 2026 and Guard troops left Chicago, Los Angeles and Portland in January 2026 after the Supreme Court's December 2025 ruling.

name: Tanzania post-election crackdown
parties: Government of President Samia Suluhu Hassan / security forces
trigger: Protests broke out on election day, 29 October 2025, after the main opposition party Chadema was barred and its leader Tundu Lissu jailed for treason, with Samia later declared winner with about 98 percent.
summary: Protests in Dar es Salaam, Mwanza, Arusha and other cities against the exclusionary 29 October 2025 election were met with live fire, an internet shutdown and mass arrests; a government commission of inquiry later counted 518 deaths while the opposition claimed far more. More than 2,000 people were arrested and Samia vowed to crush unrest 'at all cost'. The street phase ended within weeks but the crackdown on opposition continues and accountability remains absent.

history.status: As of mid-October 2026 street protest has been suppressed but the political crisis is unresolved. Opposition leader Tundu Lissu's treason trial closed on 29 September 2026 with judgment set for 6 November 2026; on 16 October a court ordered Ukonga Prison to allow him private consultations with lawyers. The government's Commission of Inquiry put post-election deaths at 518 but the president has refused to publish the report; Amnesty (April 2026) and HRW (March 2026, documenting 31 bystanders shot) say no official has been held accountable, and an ICC referral request filed in December 2025 is pending.

The largest clash came on 12 March 2025 when football fans joined the retirees: police used rubber bullets, tear gas and water cannon, over 120 were detained and photojournalist Pablo Grillo was critically injured. name: Bulgaria anti-corruption protests

trigger: A draft 2026 budget raising taxes and social-security contributions, released days before Bulgaria's eurozone entry, sparked mass youth-led protests in late November 2025.

name: Ladakh statehood protests

Wangchuk was detained under the National Security Act for six months and talks with Delhi broke down before resuming in October 2025. The next round of talks is still set for 22 October in Delhi, and no street unrest has been reported.

name: Bangladesh July uprising and transition
parties: Awami League government of Sheikh Hasina
trigger: Student protests against a quota system for government jobs in July 2024 escalated into a nationwide uprising after a lethal police crackdown.
summary: Weeks of student-led protests against job quotas turned into a mass uprising that killed several hundred people and forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee to India on 5 August 2024. A Muhammad Yunus-led interim government banned the Awami League, tried Hasina in absentia and organised the first post-uprising election in February 2026, which the BNP won in a landslide. Political violence between rival parties and sporadic mob unrest, including the December 2025 riots after the killing of activist Osman Hadi, persisted through the transition.

history.status: As of 14 October 2026 the transition set off by the uprising is largely complete: the BNP won about 209 of 300 seats in the 12 February 2026 election and Tarique Rahman was sworn in as prime minister on 17 February, replacing the Yunus interim government. The Awami League remains banned and excluded from politics and Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia in November 2025. A UK fact-finding report published 14 October 2026 found political violence continuing but mostly localised; the Awami League cites a rights-group tally of 56 deaths and over 5,000 injuries in political violence from January to June 2026.

name: Mozambique post-election protests
parties: Opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane and supporters
Frelimo government of President Daniel Chapo / security forces
trigger: The 9 October 2024 election, which the Constitutional Council awarded to Frelimo's Daniel Chapo with 65 percent, was rejected by Mondlane, who called nationwide strikes and marches after his lawyer and an aide were shot dead.
summary: Mozambique's worst post-election unrest since independence ran from October 2024 to March 2025, with marches, barricades and looting across Maputo and provincial cities met by live fire; monitoring groups counted more than 300 people shot dead and thousands arrested. Street protests subsided after Mondlane and Chapo met in March 2025, but no one has been prosecuted for the killings. The state has instead moved to try Mondlane himself over the protests.

history.status: As of 14 October 2026 the streets are quiet but the conflict has moved into the courts: the Council of State lifted Mondlane's immunity on 10 June 2026 and the Supreme Court notified him on 25 August that he will stand trial on five charges including incitement to terrorism and collective disobedience, with hearings scheduled to open on 17 November 2026. On 12 October the court rejected his appeal to have the trial broadcast live. Mondlane, who is not detained, denies the charges and says his movement's members continue to be killed.

name: Pakistan PTI protests and KP emergency rule
parties: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf and Imran Khan supporters
Federal government of Shehbaz Sharif and security forces
trigger: Imran Khan's 'final call' for a march on Islamabad in November 2024 to demand his release and overturn the disputed February 2024 election result set off a cycle of marches, lethal crackdowns and mass arrests.
summary: Since Khan's jailing in August 2023 his party has repeatedly marched on Islamabad, most violently in November 2024, when security forces cleared D-Chowk with live fire and PTI claimed multiple deaths. In autumn 2026 PTI relaunched a long march from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the government detained Khan's three sisters and hundreds of workers, and on 11 October 2026 Islamabad imposed emergency and governor's rule in KP, suspending the PTI provincial government and detaining Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. Violent protests followed across the province.

history.status: On 11 October 2026 President Zardari, on Prime Minister Sharif's advice, invoked Articles 232 and 234 to impose emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for an initial six months, citing surging terror attacks; Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and cabinet members were taken into preventive custody and PTI called it 'a coup disguised as emergency' and vowed a court challenge. On 13-14 October PTI protests in Bara, Khyber district, turned violent, with government buildings set ablaze and PTI claiming one dead and 11 injured from police fire, which authorities denied. Khan's sisters remain detained under public-order law since September.

trigger: Tchiroma declared himself winner of the 12 October 2025 presidential election before the Constitutional Council proclaimed 92-year-old Biya re-elected with 53.7 percent, sparking protests in Douala, Garoua and other cities.
summary: Protests and 'ghost town' shutdowns erupted across Cameroon after the disputed October 2025 election handed Paul Biya an eighth term; security forces fired on crowds, with the UN citing 48 deaths and civil society reporting around 2,000 arrests, and opposition figure Anicet Ekane died in custody. Tchiroma fled via Nigeria to The Gambia and the protests were crushed by December 2025. He has since pursued universal-jurisdiction complaints abroad while Cameroonian authorities threaten to prosecute him.

history.status: As of June 2026 the protest wave has been suppressed and Biya remains in power. Tchiroma, exiled in Banjul, filed complaints in June 2026 before the Paris Judicial Court and Swiss courts against Biya and officials over the post-election crackdown, and announced an 'imminent' return; in May 2026 the interior minister said Tchiroma would face legal action for inciting the violence. Crisis Group has warned the standoff remains unresolved; no fresh mass protests were reported in 2026 as of mid-October.

history.status: Four people were shot dead in Douala on 26 October 2025 and more died as results were announced on 27 October; UN sources cited 48 killed and civil society around 2,000 arrested. Tchiroma called three days of ghost-town shutdowns (3-5 November), issued a 48-hour ultimatum on 10 November for detainees' release, and fled the country as the government threatened to try him for incitement.

name: Ecuador indigenous national strike
parties: CONAIE and allied indigenous, student and union groups
trigger: President Noboa's September 2025 decree abolishing the diesel subsidy prompted CONAIE to declare an indefinite national strike on 22 September 2025.
summary: CONAIE's indefinite national strike against the removal of the diesel subsidy, mining and oil policy and cuts to health and education began on 22 September 2025, centred on the northern highlands (Imbabura, Pichincha). The government froze CONAIE's bank accounts, deployed the military and declared states of exception; three people were killed and dozens injured. CONAIE ended the strike on 22 October 2025 without concessions, and Noboa's constitutional referendum was then rejected by voters on 16 November 2025.

history.status: CONAIE announced the end of its month-long national strike on 22 October 2025, citing 'brutal repression' that left three dead and dozens injured, after Noboa threatened stronger action to clear roadblocks; no concessions were obtained. The movement pivoted to campaigning against Noboa's referendum, and on 16 November 2025 voters rejected all four questions including a constituent assembly (61% no). No renewed national strike has been reported in 2026; grievances over fuel prices and mining remain unresolved.

history.status: By mid-October 2025 the strike had lasted nearly four weeks, with road blockades across the northern Sierra, military convoys escorting fuel and food, and states of exception in several provinces. At least two protesters had been killed and more than a hundred injured; a third death followed. The government froze CONAIE's accounts and Noboa accused the movement of being financed by organised crime.

name: France student and cost-of-living protests
parties: CGT and other unions, teachers and yellow-vest groups
Government of President Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu
trigger: High-school students in Créteil, outside Paris, began blockading their lycée in mid-September 2026 over overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings and teacher shortages, and the blockades spread nationwide within weeks.
summary: What began as lycée blockades in mid-September 2026 over school conditions grew into a nationwide movement joined by teachers, the CGT union, nurses, farmers and remnants of the 2018 yellow vests, with anger widening to the cost of living and fuel prices. Early October brought clashes, arrests and school closures in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Rennes. On 17 October 2026 the largest day of action drew 550,000 people by the government's count and ended in rioting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Limoges and Bordeaux with nearly 1,800 arrests, while the Lecornu government tries to pass a deficit-cutting budget ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

history.status: On 17 October 2026 between 550,000 (Interior Ministry) and 800,000 (organisers) people marched nationwide in the movement's largest day, and rioting followed in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Limoges and Bordeaux: Marseille's town hall was breached and shops looted, Limoges' historic city hall burned, and nearly 1,800 people were arrested with more than 500 police and firefighters injured. The IGPN police inspectorate has 36 investigations open into alleged police violence. Macron addressed the nation on 18 October, while Prime Minister Lecornu blamed the far left and pressed on with a deficit-cutting budget.

name: Albania student riots against Rama government
parties: Flamingo anti-corruption movement and opposition supporters
Government of Prime Minister Edi Rama
trigger: Students who had protested peacefully for months over education costs and job prospects turned to street riots in Tirana on 13 October 2026, joining the Flamingo campaign against corruption and a Kushner-linked coastal resort.
summary: Riots broke out in Tirana on 13 October 2026 when student protests over the cost of education and poor job prospects merged with the months-old Flamingo movement opposing alleged government corruption and a luxury resort project on the southern coast linked to Jared Kushner. Over six consecutive days protesters attacked ministries, the prime minister's office, banks and police with fireworks and barricades, and police answered with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets. Prime Minister Edi Rama, in power since 2013, refuses to resign and blames a foreign hand, while the EU delegation has urged a proportionate response as Albania pursues membership by 2030.

history.status: By 18 October 2026 Tirana had seen six consecutive days of rioting. On 14 October riots lasting more than eight hours damaged at least four ministries, banks and shops, with 35 people detained and 29 injured according to AP, and protests spread to universities in Elbasan and Shkodër. The Health Ministry counted 272 people injured since 13 October, 169 of them police officers. Police are using rubber bullets, water cannon and tear gas; Prime Minister Edi Rama rules out resigning and blames foreign interference, while President Begaj and the EU delegation have appealed for calm.
